utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. If the witness could be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated. If I could remind you, Ms. Peko, of the affirmation you took when you commenced your evidence yesterday, which still applies. Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Kaufman: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Peko. Thank you for returning.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Peko, yesterday we were talking about the events of the 6th of December, 1991. I'd like to take you now to the following day, the 7th of December. But before we discuss the events of that day, could you tell us where you were working at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me think. On the 7th of December, I was working in my project bureau called Arhitekt in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 7th of December, did you receive a request of any nature?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The 7th was a Saturday, and we don't work on Saturdays. But on Monday was when I received it, and that was the 9th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that case, please tell us the nature of the request that you received on the 9th of December.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My company, the project bureau, received a request from the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments for assistance, to help them in their work to list the damages that had resulted in Dubrovnik after the 6th of December, and my director suggested that a colleague of mine, Mrs. Zdenka Bacic, and I myself, as architects, take part in listing the damages incurred. So we went to the institute that day to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this process of listing the structures that had been damaged, which institution promulgated this? The idea of which institution was this?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments did, with the proviso that UNESCO or, rather, the director general of UNESCO, Mr. Federico Mayor sent two experts to Dubrovnik to set up an office there, provisional office, representative office of UNESCO in Dubrovnik to work in cooperation with the experts at the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments in listing the damages to structures in Dubrovnik during the months of October, November, and December -- or, rather, October and November. However, they were there when the 6th of December attack on Dubrovnik took place. The UNESCO experts, as consultants who were called in, worked together with the experts of the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments and compiled a report which was entitled "Preliminary report on the damages incurred on structures during the war destructions that took place in October, November, and December of 1991."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Peko. We will seek to introduce that preliminary report in due course. The two binders -- and the two binders English translation are presently by Your Honours' chairs, but as I say, in due course. Before we get to that, I would like to ask you if you know the names of the two UNESCO officials of whom you spoke.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Mr. Colin Kaiser and Mr. Bruno Karnes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when Mr. Colin Kaiser and Mr. Bruno Karnes arrived in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They arrived in Dubrovnik towards the end of November. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you meet them for the first time?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first met them on the 9th of December, when I arrived at the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments to start working there within the frameworks of the committee set up to list the damages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, could you perhaps give us the name of some other people who took part in this exercise of listing the damages to structures in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole undertaking was done under the auspices of the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments. They have their experts, professional people to work on such matters, and the institute also had a great deal of experience working on similar work after the 1979 Dubrovnik earthquake, so that they used the -- they started compiling a list in October and went on into November. Later, with consultations with the UNESCO experts, they refined their methodology. I don't know what they did exactly, how far this was done, but the names of the people exist at the institute, and their team leader or director was Mrs. Doro Valjalo. Other members of the team working on the project were the following architects: Mr. Matko Vetma; Mr. Zvonimir Franic; Mrs. -- I think she's an art historian, Bozena Popic was her name; and an outside collaborator by the name of Slobodan Vukovic, who is also an architect by profession; and the other employees of the institute of which I can name Mr. Zeljko Franetovic, Mr. Dragan Elakovic; and those are the names I can remember just now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, don't worry, Ms. Peko, because at this point in time I'd like to formally ask to submit the preliminary report about which we are speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I believe that my learned friend has an objection, although prior to today, my learned friend had agreed to submit the whole exhibit as an exhibit in this hearing. If I might take this opportunity, Your Honours, to state that there will be one other witness who will testify before the Tribunal on the damages caused to Dubrovnik and the listing of those damages. His name is Dr. Colin Kaiser. He's due to testify next week. He had overall responsibility for the whole of the project, as you will hear, and as I told my learned friend, he will be the person to direct cross-examination concerning the methodology and the conduct of the listing process, as it were. But I would formally seek to submit the preliminary report. I will allow my learned friend to, of course, object if he wishes to object and then I would request respectfully that Your Honours allow me to reply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is what I want to address: Mr. Kaufman and I myself talked some ten days ago and discussed the report that you have before you today. We are inundated with many problems that we have and have lots of work to do so that we were only able to look through the report this weekend, and we found that there are a lot of shortcomings to it which make it impossible for us to accept in advance the tendering of that report unless we have a chance to analyse the contents of the report with the people who compiled it. Your Honours, you will see that the report you have before you in two binders is in fact a collection of individual minutes and records on the on-site examination of the structures and buildings. Each of those individual minutes was compiled by certain individuals. For example, Mrs. Peko compiled some 20 or perhaps more minutes, and every minute compiled by Mrs. Peko she signed herself and thus stands by what it says in that note, in those minutes, confirming the authenticity of the contents thereby. So we can accept having those parts of the report admitted into evidence which Mrs. Peko herself drew up and signed. As to the other parts of the report compiled by other individuals who are not in this courtroom here today, Your Honours, we would like to object to the admittance of those portions of the report into evidence at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I believe I might be able to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. suggest a compromise to the Court. I don't think it's appropriate to submit an exhibit and identify half of it as an exhibit and the other half as marked for identification, but for the ease of the Trial Chamber and for the ease of my learned friend, I passed him a week ago a table that I had drawn up of all the items within that exhibit, the site reports, which this particular witness conducted. I for my part will not take her through those individual sites one by one. I will just deal with one to show the Trial Chamber the methodology that was employed, but I have prepared a table of all the sites that this witness examined herself and I told my learned friend that it would be appropriate perhaps for him, if he wishes to cross-examine her, to cross-examine her only on those sites that she examined. The witness Dr. Kaiser will be here next week and may be cross-examined on anything else which is present in that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That being the case, it may be better to delay the formal reception into evidence of the report until we have had the evidence of Dr. Kaiser.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course if that is the course of action that the Trial Chamber is minded to take, then I cannot object, but I would ask, for the sake of convenience, for it to be admitted as an exhibit at this point in time. I'm quite happy to give Your Honours the table. Once again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But its admission, by the sound, will really depend upon the evidence of a witness yet to come, for some part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the relevance of this exhibit has been established, but I take Your Honour's point. If I may just consult with my learned leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I would just like for the record to reflect, whilst appreciating everything, of course, that the Trial Chamber has said, and agreeing to the course of action proposed by the Trial Chamber, I would respectfully request the record reflect, however, that this witness took part in the process of listing these buildings. She's familiar with the methodology that was employed. She's familiar with the contents of the report by virtue of being a member of the institute itself, and therefore we believe that the exhibit could be submitted through this witness, but if the Court is minded to take that course of action, then for the sake of convenience we will of course agree and oblige the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What I suggest, Mr. Kaufman, is that the witness identify by name or other means the buildings that are the subject of the report for which she can personally vouch so that the record is clear as to that. I would propose that the full report be at the moment marked for identification in the anticipation that, on the basis that you have indicated, Dr. Kaiser will be able to make good the balance of the report and it will be received then in due course. Should there be some unforeseen slip-up and we are left without Dr. Kaiser or evidence to deal with the balance of the report, the record would then provide a basis upon which the Chamber could accept into evidence at least that part of the report which has been identified as the work of Mrs. Peko. For the moment, I think marked for identification is the safe way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I'm obliged to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I think that deals with your concern, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I deeply respect what you have just said. You presented your viewpoint before I was about to offer a compromise solution, perhaps, to this problem. My learned colleague -- with the Court's indulgence, I would like to present our proposal, if I might be allowed to do that. My learned colleague drew up a list of those parts of the report which were compiled by Mrs. Peko herself and which she signed herself. My proposal was that those portions that he marked on this entire document, and they have ERN numbers both in the B/C/S and the English version, that they be tendered into evidence as exhibits while the rest of the documents, the rest of the report will be decided on in due course. So that's what I wanted, just to put that proposal forward as a compromise solution. Of course it is up to you, Your Honours, to decide how we shall proceed, and we shall, of course, abide by your decisions and fully respect them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petkovic, for your spirit of cooperation. What the Chamber has in mind is to avoid part of this report being an exhibit and not the whole of it. What the Chamber proposes, I think, would achieve what each of you have in mind but in a way that would minimise the problem for the record of what is and what is not an exhibit by simply marking, at the moment, for identification the whole report, but the evidence of Ms. Peko would provide a basis later for the admission of those parts which you have just mentioned should it be necessary for some unforeseen reason to tender only part of the report as an exhibit. But at the moment it would be neater and tidier if the whole report were admitted as an exhibit, and that must await the evidence of Dr. Kaiser. So we'll proceed on that basis, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. To that end, Your Honour, I have the table of sites examined by Ms. Peko. I would respectfully ask the usher, if possible, to circulate this table. Could the exhibit -- sorry. Could the item marked Prosecution Exhibit 35 for the purpose of the pre-trial brief, i.e., the two bundles in B/C/S, be placed before the witness, if possible. The purpose, of course, being the formal identification and no more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Peko, could you open the first of those bundles, please. Do those two bundles comprise the preliminary report of which we were speaking?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They're here. For example, this particular structure, the Franciscan Monastery, the Church of St. Spaso, Our Saviour. Perhaps I could tell you something about the methodology, because this is just part of the whole of the entire undertaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, Ms. Peko, we have to deal with the legal formalities, if that's okay by you. If you could open perhaps the second bundle and just identify that that as well forms part of the preliminary report.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's it. Yes, that is part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, pursuant to Your Honours' decision, I wonder if this exhibit could be marked for identification formally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document will be marked P51 ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Peko, please look at the sheet of A4 that I have handed out. The far right column is marked "Site," and there are a list of sites going all the way down. Does that comprise the list of sites that you examined?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. The numbers correspond to the areas where I worked, so I assume that all the buildings mentioned on the right-hand side -- I mean, I think all of this is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the documents are before the Court, Ms. Peko. I can assure you that --

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the matter will be examined in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, for Your Honours' convenience, perhaps I could explain this table. The witness in a few moments will testify as to what the various terms mean and how the items were split up, but for Your Honours' convenience - and this is a matter of OTP significance so perhaps I could explain it - the column marked "ERN" is the exhibit number. Your Honours will see that there is a B/C/S number and a number given for the English translation. Those may be used by Your Honours for convenience purposes in order to find the relevant site. As you will notice in the bundles before you, there are -- every page is numbered. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Peko, looking at this sheet, there is a term entitled "Insula". This is the second column along. What is an insula?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of the town of Dubrovnik within the old city walls is divided into 17 insulas. This system was accepted as far back as the time when the basic documents about Dubrovnik were compiled. Then this was also used after the earthquake in 1979, and it was used again now. Since this system makes it possible to find one's way easily, it is still the principle governing the division of the city. So we dealt with 17 insulas of the Old City. And then there was a separate insula, number 18 I think it was, and that is Placa, and that is the main street in town. And then a separate insula were the Old City walls of Dubrovnik. So there were a total of 19 entities that were dealt with. So the insulas are marked here, and the particular facilities within them that are dealt with separately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for clarification, the Old Town of Dubrovnik comprises 19 insula, or insulae, perhaps. Can you confirm that, please?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Absolutely. I'm just telling you that this was done in terms of our line of work when dealing with the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you and your fellow team members were sent out to these various insulae and asked to survey what you saw there and what damages you saw incurred by the various sites. What were you told to look out for in particular?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our duty was, since I was a member of the institution that came there to help, and I worked from the 9th until the 18th of December, at the very outset I wanted to familiarise myself with the methodology and with the deadlines involved for producing the documents that were to pertain to the buildings that I was supposed to deal with. Of course, this methodology consists of several elements. Specifically, I received instructions as to how I was supposed to work in the field. I had a particular form, and then there were certain questions that I was supposed to answer. So I had to fill out the form, basically. Basic information was to be provided about the building itself, the time of inspection, the time when the damage was sustained, the description of the damage, and this -- and then the category involved. I would submit this document to the institute afterwards so that the authors of the preliminary report would then bring all of these forms together and show this on maps. One map had to do -- deal with classification of damages, and the other one had to do with the type and place of damages incurred. My duty was to fill out the forms in the field, so to speak, and to hand them over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Peko, you talked about the category involved. What do you mean by "category"?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: While the methodology was being developed, the categories fell into four different groups, namely, this had to do with four different types of damage sustained. The first category were fully destroyed buildings. How should I put this? That is the highest level of damage. Then the second category were buildings where there were damaged walls and roofs. The third category were buildings that had only their roof destroyed or only their walls, but not both. And the fourth category were buildings with minor damage sustained. That is to say these were buildings that were often indirectly damaged. So that was what was shown. As for the type of damage, there were other signs, and this was shown on a separate map. It had to do with direct damage on roofs and walls, direct damage on roofs, and then totally burned buildings, and then indirect damage of walls, indirect damage sustained by roofs, and buildings that were partially burned up. All the actual localities are depicted on a map, and also the type of damage sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser will deal with that particular map, Ms. Peko, but since earlier you asked us to allow you to explain something about your particular methodology and one of the buildings that you inspected, perhaps this is a convenient opportunity to deal with the Franciscan Monastery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: For this end, Your Honour, so Your Honours don't have to fumble your way through the binders, I have prepared this particular part of the binders in a separate handout. I would request that they be circulated. This is purely for convenience sake. This item need not be assigned an exhibit number at all. Your Honour, I would request that the B/C/S version actually be in front of the Bench because there are diagrams and maps contained in that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Peko, working from the version in B/C/S, if you could look at the front page. We see that this is in fact, I believe, the second volume of the preliminary report. Is that correct? The cover page, please, Ms. Peko. The front page.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the preliminary report. Yes, that's the cover page, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there are the number 1/2?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to the next page. There is a map there. What's that map? What does that show?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a map of Dubrovnik depicting the insulae. Insula number 1 is where the Franciscan Monastery is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now if you could turn, please, to the fourth page, the page marked 01069151.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I wonder if this item could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we have lots of different geometrical shapes here, Ms. Peko. Perhaps you could take us through what we see on this particular map. First of all, what does it portray?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is part of the map that pertains to insula 1. All the maps of all the insulas actually make up the map that depicts all the damage sustained. We see here the markings of various localities and the damage sustained. I have to mention that the signs, the markings used here, are symbols, actually. They are not supposed to specifically or precisely denote the area of the damage involved. This was used for the entire area of the entire town. I can say that the small circles, the black dots, denote damages sustained by the facades or horizontal surfaces. The triangles, the black triangles denote direct hits on roofs. So those are direct hits. The empty triangles, so to speak, denote indirect hits. And then there is yet another symbol for indirect damage sustained by facades, the very small dots. So that is basically the damage that was sustained by this insula and then recorded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this complex, is this the Franciscan Monastery?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the entire compound of the Franciscan Monastery, and a fountain that I did not deal with myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, for Your Honours' convenience --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can show it, actually. This is the entire compound of the Franciscan Monastery. This is it. This is the Church of Our Saviour here, and this is the fountain, Onofrijeva Fountain, but that was dealt with by some other colleague of mine. All of that is insula number 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe if we look at the map on page 01069150, which is the third page, we can see numbers which relate to the subdivision of the Franciscan Monastery into smaller subsites; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. My intention was to show the damage in the clearest possible way, So that is why I had it grouped this way. So certain parts of certain buildings were given a number. Often the division into insulae corresponds with the land survey divisions that had existed beforehand. I wanted to show the damage sustained on parts of individual buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So looking at this map and from your previous answer, the only subsite that you did not examine in this site, Franciscan Monastery and its church, was basically number 14, the fountain.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct, correct. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we may turn to -- just for the sake of example, so you could tell us your methodology, in the B/C/S version to page 01069153, and in the English version, which is probably the version which will be the most easy for the Bench to refer to, it's draft translation L0060284. Now, the number, I believe, relates to the subsite, does it not? It's called brodj, I think, in B/C/S. Broj, I apologise for my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the number of the insula and the number of the particular building within the insula. This is the cloister of the Franciscan Monastery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The location, type of object, date and hour of inspection are fairly self-explanatory. I'd like to ask you about the date of the incident. How did you know the date of the incident for the purposes of filling out the form?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is recommended, or it was recommended then when we were working on these buildings, that we should collect all available information, everything that you can see by way of changes in the physical state of the building, since we are professionals in this area, but we were also supposed to ask the people using the actual building for all the information they may have had. So I used information that I got from the monks in the monastery. They were there during the attack when the building was damaged, and of course they were trying to protect it from the fire spreading from the neighbouring buildings, inter alia. They gave me information about all of this. The date is not really controversial because it is known that it was precisely on the 6th of December that the largest number of projectiles were fired at the Franciscan Monastery, and that is when it sustained most of the damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But from what I understand, you would, at least on some of the occasions, receive the information from people who had been within the building itself when it was hit, or thereby, near thereby.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's right. Yes, of course. They recorded all the damage sustained by their building. Perhaps not on the very same day, but the situation position was such that they were in a position to do so. I was also informed by them about the type of projectiles that had hit the building involved. The most important task was to identify the actual damage incurred and to categorise it. I have to note one more thing, that this is a preliminary report, so it is an introductory report, so to speak, and then it was followed by more detailed processing. Of course, this more detailed processing involved an estimate of the damage sustained and possible reconstruction, and that was not an issue at that point in time. However, it was very hard for me in the specific case of the Franciscan Monastery. I mean, I had to record only the physical damage sustained rather than all the true damage sustained by such an important historical monument. And that is a different thing from a damage sustained by a plain old wall. It was very hard for me, but I did my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean, Ms. Peko, when you state that true damage was sustained by an important historical monument as opposed to physical damage?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Franciscan Monastery was hit by 37 projectiles. Not to go into the exact figures involved, some of them hit the cloister of the Franciscan Monastery. That is the internal courtyard that is considered to be one of the most valuable sites within our historical and cultural heritage in Dubrovnik. It dates back to the 14th century. It is of exceptional architectural and historical value. Parts of this cloister consist of architectural and sculptural plastic which is impossible to restore if it is damaged, because all the parts of the pillars there are quite different. This building dates back to the 14th century. That is to say, a period of time from which we have very few buildings left because Dubrovnik experienced a major earthquake in the 17th century. This was created by top masters, local people. And regardless of the calibre of the projectile that had hit the building and parts of it, it involved the kind of damage that was irreparable. And then, for example, parts of the pavement were hit. It is possible to restore it but it will never be the same thing. It will never be the authentic monument that it once was. So we simply cannot talk about this kind of damage in terms of parts of this monument. I don't know whether I was clear enough really. Perhaps I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were perfectly clear, Ms. Peko. Thank you. Now, the last question I want to ask you -- sorry, just two more short questions on this report. The type of projectile you record here as being 82 millimetres and 120-millimetres mortar bombs. Now, you said that in some circumstances you would be told what type of shell had fallen, or projectile. What knowledge did you have of the types of projectiles that were found in these sites? Of course I appreciate you're not an artillery expert, so confine it to what you know and what you saw.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the projectiles, I indeed am no expert. I wouldn't want to go into that. As a matter of fact, I find this repulsive. But it is a fact that in this particular case I spent some ten days after the 6th of December before coming to inspect these buildings and streets. By then, all the damage had been sustained by the projectiles themselves and by other buildings that had fallen. All the people who lived in town or worked in town in various buildings kept parts of the projectiles that fell. So it is certain that these were the projectiles that were shown to me within the monastery itself. Specifically, I know very little about this. However, concerning the remains of mortar shells and the like, I know that 80-millimetre and 120-millimetre shells involve a change of calibre, and that can easily be identified. I mean, that can be seen. I don't know if I should add anything to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, back in 1991, did you have an opportunity to compare fragments of shells that you found, shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, sometimes we weren't able to find them all, but generally they were saved in buildings. They were lodged in the buildings, and we called them the tails of the projectiles, that is the bottom end of the projectile. And they had sort of wing-like attachments. So parts of shrapnel of this kind were lodged in the structures that they damaged, so I was able to see them. I saw the remains of these. Of course, I wasn't well-versed in the different types of projectiles, but as I say, I had an opportunity to hold these in my hands and to see them lodged in the structures themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your answer, Ms. Peko, I understand it's difficult for you to talk about this, so my last question is simply to summarise the state of affairs. I believe that the type of projectile entry on the form was compiled on the basis of what you were told and sometimes on the basis of what you saw. Would that be a fair summary of what you've said?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was basically and mostly on the basis of what I saw in the largest number of cases. However, might I just be allowed to add something here? The projectiles themselves, as far as I was concerned, were of lesser importance. What was important to me was the actual damage done, and you can be absolutely certain that I was able to differentiate between direct hits and indirect hits and the damage the two incurred. Perhaps I was wrong in thinking that way, but that was the first thing I had in mind when I went to examine the site.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain how you could distinguish, as you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could see the point at which the projectile hit the structure, and I'll show you that with the help of this form. For example, on the terrace of the cloister. I'll take that example to explain what I mean. It is 010695.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 9165. Yes. Ms. Peko, looking at that photograph 01069165. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a direct hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, once again, Ms. Peko, I don't want to go into any -- too much detail on that because as we've said, you are not an artillery expert, but I thank you for that. And I take it although you're not an expert, that was how you catalogued a direct hit?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that was what you call a direct hit today, that was presumably how you would have recorded it.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Yes. An indirect hit had different graphics. It looked differently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again, we won't trouble you with that at the moment because there will be someone else who will come and give evidence about that. And finally, you would, of course, on this form list the category of damage. And in this particular instance that's to be found on the draft English translation at L0060285. In this particular instance, the subsite 1, the damage was category 2 damage. Thank you. If you could put that exhibit aside now -- that item aside.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm conscious of the time. I'm bringing the evidence in chief to a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Peko, being an architect who worked in the Dubrovnik municipality, I take it you were familiar with the whole of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dubrovnik, the present-day town of Dubrovnik, has the narrow inner circle from Kantafiga to St. Jakov. And within that framework or within that circle you will find the Old Town nucleus of Dubrovnik and Gruz, Lapad, and Sveti Jakov being the outlining areas. I know the area well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And being an architect familiar with buildings and the uses that buildings are put to in the region of Dubrovnik, I would take it you would know what buildings were devoted to military uses and what buildings were devoted to civilian uses.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no buildings that are devoted to military uses in Dubrovnik. What there is were the Austro-Hungarian barracks that were left empty in 1960 something, and since then there were no military buildings within the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the question might seem a bit facile after I received your response, but could you tell us if you saw any military installations, weapons of any sort in October, November, December 1991?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw nothing like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Peko, there is just one final clarification question which arose out of the transcript yesterday and then I will conclude. The transcripts of yesterday's hearing - for the sake of the record, page 74, line 22 - you talked about Dubrovnik being protected. Which part of Dubrovnik did you mean when you said that Dubrovnik was protected?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first of all meant the protection of Dubrovnik as a cultural monument generally. Dubrovnik within its outer walls and including the town walls and the Lovrijenac and Revelin fortresses outside the wall perimeter are considered to be an entity and the highest, the top category of cultural monument. Dubrovnik was protected from the very establishment of the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments in Dubrovnik. It enjoyed protection. From 1979 onwards, it was listed as a World Heritage Site attached to UNESCO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Peko, thank you very much. I most appreciate your assistance. You will be asked some questions by the Defence now, but maybe, Your Honours, this is an appropriate point for a break. I don't know. Unless it's too early for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is, I think, a little early. We will start cross-examination now, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mrs. Peko. I am attorney Vladimir Petrovic, and I'm going to be asking you some questions in connection with what you were discussing with my learned colleague. Tell me, please, the time before October 1991, can you describe for me where the house you lived in was actually located. What kind of building was it and where was it situated?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a residential building comprising of several apartments in the Zlatni Potok settlement in Dubrovnik, a housing estate in the area of Sveti Jakov, to the east of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For purposes of orientation, tell us, please, near the building you lived in there were any facilities that stand out, like a hotel, for example, or any landmarks of that kind.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the one side to the east is the Belvedere Hotel, and to the west, between my building and the Old Town itself, is the Argentina and Excelsior hotels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, the building you lived in, is it along the coast, near the coast, or as you said yesterday, on the slopes of Mount Srdj?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite a way away from the coast. It is above the upper town road, more inland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you mentioned a moment ago in response to my learned colleague's question something. Do you remember where the barracks in Dubrovnik were up until the 1960s?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Gruz. It's still a barracks, but it's not used as a barracks. The barracks stands as a building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from the 1960s up until the beginning of the events that took place in the 1990s, is it true and correct that not a single unit was stationed, of the JNA, in Dubrovnik at that time, the army of the day?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was not a single unit stationed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also right that very rarely in Dubrovnik up until 1990, the times that we're talking about, were you able to encounter in town or anywhere else any JNA soldiers, because there weren't any there?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There weren't any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it -- or let me ask you this way: Did you take part in the procedure of including Dubrovnik into the list of World Heritage Sites in the 1970s? Did you take part in that?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an employee of the Institute for Protection, probably you could say I did, however, the main documents for it to be listed and to be -- for Dubrovnik to be put forward as a candidate to become a World Heritage Site was done by the Institute for Art in Zagreb, headed by Professor Milan Prelog [phoen]. So the associates of the institute and the employees of the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments worked together and participated together in putting forward Dubrovnik as a candidate for a World Heritage Site, and they compiled all the supporting documents for that to be made possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you remember whether one of the conditions for listing Dubrovnik as a World Heritage Site was that it should be a demilitarised town? That means a town in which there would be no military units stationed. Was that one of the prerequisites?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. Dubrovnik had to satisfy very high criteria and standards in the sense of being authentic and well-preserved in the sense of its artistic values and structural values, and I know, for example, that the fact that it was a living town, a live old town, was a very noteworthy factor, a point in its favour, and that throughout its existence it always catered to the needs of its inhabitants. And the relationship of those inhabitants and its citizens towards the cultural values was taken note of. May I be allowed to finish, please? Now, since for urban entities of that kind you have to have -- you have to comply with international documents dealing with protection that were the result of UNESCO efforts and United Nations efforts generally, I can just assume that there was something along the lines of what you were saying, but I can't actually Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. claim that myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, yesterday in respond to a question from my learned colleague, you talked about how the process of protection was established, was set up. Tell me, please, in this procedure, in determining the protection of structures and buildings, is there any difference between the different edifices or, rather, are all edifices equally -- enjoy equal protection or is there a grade and category as to which enjoys greater protection and which does not?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely right. I said yesterday that the protection of edifices, of structures, was based on a document which was drawn up on the basis of evaluation and assessment. And when I said that, I had in mind a series of procedures that are put in place in order to compile documents of that kind. Research is conducted in order to establish the state of a building, the state of a structure, and its value and worth, that is to say the -- not only the artistic value but all the other points according to which it can enjoy protection as a protected site. Of course, those pre-conditions have different categories as well, and the entire Dubrovnik area or the Old Town nucleus of Dubrovnik is an entity that enjoyed protection very early on because its value is undoubtable. However, within that entity, of course, within that nucleus, certain structures enjoy a higher category, others enjoy a lower category.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, but may I ask you to be a bit briefer in your answers because I know that our time is limited. So would you try and be as concise as possible. Thank you for your understanding, because we are faced with time constraints, of course. Now, you mentioned yesterday the historical urban entity. So can you just -- and you explained a moment ago when asked by my learned colleague what this means, what you mean by the historical urban entity, that is to say the old town, the walls. What else?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be it. It would be the Old Town nucleus within the walls; the Lovrijenac fortress, which is outside the murals; the Revelin fortress, which can be considered to be part of the fortification wall; and the complex of the city lazareti, and they enjoy protection -- quarantine cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have lived in Dubrovnik your whole life, and you've just mentioned the different localities now, and you talked about this broader belt around the town. Could you please tell us the streets that delineate this broader town belt. Or perhaps you'd find it easier with a map, working with a map.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Lazarina Street on the east, Volantina on the west, Jadranska Ceska Street on the south side, that is to say the sea side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to show us Exhibit P11. P11, please. Could you show that to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since it's large map and can't fit into the overhead projector, for the record, please, would you repeat the streets you mentioned earlier on, and then we'll find a way of showing them. So could you take a look at the map, tell me the streets again for the record, and then we'll be able to fold the map and find the streets and place them on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just seek clarification? I'm telling you about something that we recognised at the time I worked in the institute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we talk about this area, we don't imply strict protection for the city of Dubrovnik. It is protection only in the case of any construction work going on in the area, to stipulate the limitations and to prevent any building that would damage the aspect of the town. However, everything today is regulated by the town plans. So I think --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take this step-by-step.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I'm talking about protection of the Old Town, the inner city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was asking you about the time you worked at the institute, and you told us that a moment ago. So just tell me -- repeat the names of the streets for the record, for the transcript, if possible, and then we'll try and find them on the map as well. If you can't see them, it doesn't matter. We'll move on. Could you read out the names, please.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lazarina above the Excelsior Hotel. Lazarina above the Excelsior hotel. And Volantina on the west. And on the other side is the Adriatic Motorway, as it's called.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We won't be needing the map any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you said a moment ago that the lazareti fortress makes up part of the ancient history of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a fortress, it's a quarantine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do apologise. I meant Lovrijenac fortress.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that that makes up the component part of the city along the walls.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now if my orientation serves me, how far is Lovrijenac from Bokar? That is the furthest point.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 50 metres. Perhaps. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the status is today of the Old Town surroundings, walls?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Peko, let us just summarise. Just before the break, if I understood you correctly, we established that the area that is under UNESCO protection is the one that includes the Old Town underneath the walls, Lovrijenac, Revelin, and the lazareti quarantine. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what is the status of the Imperial fortress on Mount Srdj in terms of monument protection?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wish to say that the basic tenets related to monument protection are included in documents relevant to that. The Imperial fortress dates back to the Austro-Hungarian rule, and I don't know whether it was registered as a historical or cultural monument, and I don't know what the category of this particular landmark is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether it's a cultural monument at all or not?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where this piece of information can be obtained, that is to say, what the status of the Imperial fortress is, where this is registered, who decides about this, where the relevant documents are, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Protection Institute, which is now called the Protection of the Cultural Heritage, which is in Dubrovnik, decides on all such matters and all of the documents are there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember in those days, in the autumn of 1991, how many attacks were there against the Old Town of Dubrovnik? Can you remember approximately or exactly?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 23rd and the 24th of October, then between the 8th and 13th of November, and on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me exactly or approximately on the 23rd and the 24th of October how many shells fell on the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give me an approximation, a tentative figure?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly. I really didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me about the period between the 8th and the 13th of November? How many shells fell on the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the report refers to over 100. Look at that. Look at the figures provided by the Institute for the Protection of Monuments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to the best of your knowledge, about 100 in that period between Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the 8th and the 13th of November?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's according to the report that they had from that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your impression? You were in town at the time, the 13th of November. What was your impression? What was your estimate?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was that a great many of them fell, especially on the 10th. I mean, we practically spent all of those five days lying on the floor, and we would not have done that if shells were not falling very often. We barely managed to get out of the house, during the night, for the most part, to get something, but during the day we would not leave the house where we had found shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your estimate? How many shells fell on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again my estimate is based on an estimate or, rather, a survey of the total damage included in the report, the preliminary report. The figure of 1.000 or even more is referred to there. It was a cannonade, I mean --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We understood that. So I'm just asking you to answer my specific questions. Tell me, am I right if I say that every projectile that falls on the Old Town involves damage? If it falls on the pavement, on a building, on a wall, there is no place for it to fall without causing damage; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know how many buildings were hit in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course I understand that. Of course you don't know the exact number, but could you give me an approximation? If you can. I mean, if you cannot, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot. Not exactly. I know the first hit in Boskoviceva Street, and we were astonished by that. This was the beginning, this was the first attack on town. And then also the museum Rupe was damaged and buildings around Boskoviceva Street, and the harbour. I cannot give you the exact number, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how many buildings were hit in the period between the 8th and the 13th of November? You said that about 100 shells fell. So that's probably the number of damage cases as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite a few fell. Quite a bit in town, quite a bit in the harbour, quite a bit in the city walls. Then individual buildings were damaged within the town but I cannot give you an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask that we move on to the preliminary report that my learned friend showed you awhile ago, and I think it would be easier both for you and me if the lady would be given the B/C/S versions of this exhibit. I would like to ask you to take a look at the first binder in the B/C/S. The big black binder next to you. Could you please look at this page that is at the very outset. The last three figures are 058. The last three figures are 058.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 412 are the last three figures in the English version, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, is this the page where we can see who drafted the report that we're discussing today?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in the upper part, is there mention of the institution that compiled it?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let us say for the transcript the Republic of Croatia, the Institute for the Protection of Cultural and Natural Landmarks in Dubrovnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a look at this list now, the list of persons. So Mr. Vetma Matko is one name, and it says that's the leader of the group. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what was his role in this entire project?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is an employee of the Institute for Protection of Cultural Monuments, an architect who has worked on conservation for a long time. For a while we worked together, he was a co-worker of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of his working experience, is that the reason why he was appointed leader of this group?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I assumed it is because of his professional qualifications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what I am asking. Is it because of his working experience and his professional qualifications that he was appointed leader?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, when you look at this list, would I be right to say that all these persons are architects, historians of art? Are there any other professions represented? We see photographers too.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Architectural technicians, photographers, and then our colleague Mr. Elakovic, he is an ethnologist with a long, long career in the protection of monuments. The rest are architects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at page 061. Those are the last three figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a bit further on, Your Honour. It is L00611414 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, what was the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 061 in B/C/S. Those are the last three figures.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I've found it now. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what is this text that we see here? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an introductory text in the preliminary report. So it's an introduction, a preface. Mrs. Doroteja Valjalo signed it, and at that time she was director of that Institution for the Protection of Cultural Monuments, so the basic figures are there and the methodology too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She signed it on behalf of the institution where she worked, I assume.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mrs. Valjalo participate in the elaboration of this report? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. She was the director of the institute. She was present. I cannot say that she coordinated it, but probably up to a point in terms of deadlines and the general approach to this endeavour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would you agree that this report was compiled by persons who were professionals trained for this particular job?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You believe that this report is reliable and accurate in terms of its content?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Bearing in mind the circumstances under which it was compiled. It was compiled within a month's time. There was always an imminent threat of war and further attacks against Dubrovnik. It was also done on the basis of the experience we had in reporting after the earthquake in Dubrovnik. And the heading itself says that this is a preliminary report, and therefore it can be amended later and perhaps it would involve more accurate indicators of the damage sustained and the ways in which it can be redressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, who divided these persons into groups, people who were working on it? Who specifically assigned you to work on the insulae that you talked abut here today?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, immediately after the 6th of December, people at the institute started working on this straight away. I was involved on the 9th. I don't know exactly who gave me this assignment for my particular line of work, but I think that some colleagues had already started working and that these were the buildings that had not been dealt with until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you hand your reports to?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the institute. It wasn't important at a personal level who you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were supposed to give them to. One of the leaders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was someone who collected these reports; right?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it? Were these the people who were mentioned here as the authors?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very probably. There is no reason for me to hand this in to colleagues who were in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was only logical that I should give it to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you gave it to one of the authors. Let me just remind you, for the transcript, Matko Vetma, Mr. Zvonimir Franic, Bozena Popic, and Slobodan Vukovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, someone who was at the institute at that point in time. They worked at various buildings too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The authors are these four persons whose names I just read out now. That's what it says on this page.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Involving consultations with colleagues from UNESCO too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was a final report ever written?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, yes. There was a state commission that later worked on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this final report?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I can just say that a report had been made concerning the damage sustained by all buildings irrespective of protection. There was a programme of reconstruction and a priority plan that had to deal with reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not see the final report?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the final report contains?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you anything about it because I don't work at that institution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear of any differences between the preliminary report and this final report?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was any record of the damage sustained by the Old City in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me who did this and how?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again it was the Institute for Protection of Cultural Monuments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a collective report for May 1992 there perhaps?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't -- it wasn't only in May. It was in June, July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but in 1992 is there an overall collective, comprehensive report?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, but I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when you were in situ, what did you do? You arrive at the site, at the structure, then what do you do next? Could you describe your job, what you do once you're in the field.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to tour the whole structure, see the point of damage, describe it, and determine the degree of damage incurred and the category, give it a category.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take notes while you did this kind of work?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make sketches of the damage itself?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the work I did with damaged structures, after the war I worked on ten to 12 projects in all, of that type. I did make sketches in August 1992, and it was damage to the stone plastics or carvings. That's where I did the sketches, but not for the preliminary report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you enter the structure?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go into every structure that you were assigned to investigate?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I could go into one of them, one of the buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember why?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were no inhabitants there any more, it was closed off, so we were just able to record the external damages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember which building that was?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were the photographs attached to the report taken?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photographs were taken parallelly with the teams recording the damages. At the same time. They were in situ at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So does that mean that the photographer was part of your team as well?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, photographers were part of the team, but as there were just two of them, they weren't able to go with each team. As I said, they recorded the damages even before I turned up to do my particular assignment in recording the damages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, who would tell the photographers what to photograph if they weren't with you all the time? There were six or seven teams and there were just two photographers, as you told us, so who tells them what to -- what photos to take?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the photographers are professionals and well able to recognise damages themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the photographers made assessments and evaluations of their own as to what they thought was important and should be documented?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they recognised the damage, of course, and then photographed it. They photographed the damages, and that's all, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how did they know what to take photographs of if they hadn't received instructions from you?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milenko Mojas, for example, has many years of experience working in the Institute for Cultural Monuments, and he's certainly able to recognise damage when he sees it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in all cases that were the subject of your investigations was there a written report always attended by photographs, with photographs as supporting material? Was that always the case?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have a building or structure, you provide a complete description of the damage incurred, you support it with photographs. They don't always show everything, but photographs do show some of the damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What I would like to know is how you make the selections. Why do you photograph some of the damage and not other damage?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would entail far greater work and a much lengthier report. The report would be a very thick one. So what we did was to provide preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the final report, does that contain photographs of each and every piece of damage?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't actually say, but certainly. I'm quite sure it does. It's how we do our work. You have a textual description, you have the graphics of it, and you have photographs to bear out what you have described so I'm quite sure, although I can't say for sure, I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, wouldn't photographs be the best evidence of the damage you noted in the preliminary report, in the work you did?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what to say to that. I wrote the textual description, and the description, for instance, of the cloister of the Franciscan Monastery would merit at least 20 pages of reporting. Perhaps 20 would be too much, but at least ten pages of the report would have to be devoted to the cloister of the Franciscan Monastery. But you have to be concise in order to provide a picture and image of the damage incurred. This wasn't done in that detail. We didn't have sufficient time to go into all those details, but what I wrote corresponds to the truth in absolute terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that in all the structures except one you were able to go into them to take a look round, to look at the construction. Describe what you look for and examine when you go into a structure in order to be able to write your report.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You first of all look at the outside damage. That is a basic indicator, which is always reflected in the internal part of the structure. You don't go to the cellar or basement if the roof has been damaged. Then you would go to the roof section, and you see that the partitioning walls, for example, have been toppled. You look at the portal, you look at the facades, you look at the cracks and superficial craters and things of that type. So you look at the series of damages that result from the impact that has occurred and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you record the cracks on the walls, for example; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You mention cracks in your report if they're visible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you record any plaster that has fallen off the walls?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, plaster is minor damage. That's not so important. The important thing for me is visible cracks on the facades, destruction to the constructual and structural elements, the bearing walls, the roof construction, et cetera, and then the more minor damages that attend these major damages. So if you have a strong impact, you will have all the attending damages to the surface of the wall, to the partitioning walls, to the facade, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you look at the construction first.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you look at the roof construction.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you look at the attending damages.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all those that are visible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, when you went in the field, in situ, did you have any documents with you telling you who the property belonged to, any land registry information or anything of that kind, any documents when you went on site?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. All I had was the formulas, and I conducted my investigation on the basis of the points stipulated in the forms. It doesn't matter who the structure belongs to; what matters is the damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, would you allow me to be the judge of that, the important things for my case. Tell me what you do next. You conduct this analysis or investigation of the structure. Where do you fill the forms in?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fill the form in in my on handwriting on the spot, straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is on the spot that you complete your job. You then hand in your formula -- your form, and that's where your job finishes, is that right, once you have completed the form?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. On the basis of the number of the structure which I had given to me beforehand, once I am given the assignment. Everything else is done on the spot, in situ. Perhaps I would think about the category I would assign to the damage and structure, but there wasn't much to think about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what guides you in determining the category?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the area in which the damage takes place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what point in time do you decide what category to give a certain structure; on the spot, later on when you go back to your institute, or when?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mostly on the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then that report is typed out by someone else; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The report that you handed over in written -- in your handwriting to the institute.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the chance of looking through the typed-out copy of your report?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know when I had a chance of doing that exactly. I suppose before it was bound, before binding was given it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever in fact have a chance to look through the typed-out report?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you an exact time. Probably before the binding took place, when the final work in drawing up the forms was completed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
